title: The Valley Governorship
notebook: Lucjan Ostrava has kept the valley roads patrolled and the permit office open, and the Halden villages have been quiet under him for years.
Ilse Marr teaches in a village school, speaks Dravenni in her classroom, and has asked the ministry for bilingual readers that never arrived.
Teren Vashko wants the valleys to govern themselves. Appointing him would answer a question the capital has never let the valleys ask, and it could also end the Republic's hold on the north.

narrative.text: The gendarmerie headquarters in Halden was built to hold a town's worth of prisoners, and it now houses the man who runs the valleys. At the gate a queue of farmers waits at the permit office with folded papers in their hands. You are taken up a stone stairwell to a room with a map of the valleys on the wall, every road inked in red and every checkpoint marked with a small cross. Through the window the Halden iron mines stand shuttered, their headframes grey against a low sky. Beyond the ridge, the Tyvaren border is a day's ride north. Vyktor takes in the room the way he takes in everything, without appearing to look.

There has been no fire in a schoolhouse in this valley for a long time, Chancellor, and no stone thrown at a gendarme that was not answered the same week. The roads are patrolled because the roads carry the harvest, and the permits are required because a valley where nobody knows who is passing through is a valley where the border becomes a rumor by spring. That is not cruelty. It is procedure, and procedure is the only thing these people have been offered that did not come with a rifle attached.

I will not use the word you may have been given in the capital, and I will not use it in this room. I govern the valleys the way a gendarmerie governs a district that has had three bad winters in succession. Leave me the permits, the patrols, and the right to close a road when a crowd gathers, and the valleys will stay as quiet as they are today. Take those away and I cannot tell you what the spring will bring.

Ostrava rises and buttons his coat with the precision of a man who has buttoned it for most of his life. He inclines his head but does not offer his hand. He says he will wait downstairs in case you have questions, and he says it in a way that makes clear he does not expect any. The door closes behind him. In the courtyard a gendarme salutes, and a car pulls away toward the north road, throwing grit that drifts across the glass. Vyktor waits until the engine has faded before he speaks.

Ostrava's case is accurate as far as it goes, and it is the one the capital has relied on for a decade. The valleys are quiet and the roads are safe for the harvest carts. But the quiet is held down rather than settled. A lid keeps a pot from boiling, and it does nothing about what is inside. Halvek appointed every governor in this province, and each of them answered to his office first and to the valleys second, if at all. Ostrava is the most capable of them, and that is the reason to be careful.

Marr is a different kind of answer. She speaks Dravenni in her classroom and Veltrian in the Assembly, and the villages trust her because she has never pretended the language was a problem. She would be a Dravenni governor who still answers to the Republic. Vashko would be a governor who might not answer to Veltria at all. Appointing him is either the reconciliation this province has waited for or the first step toward losing it, and you will not know which until it is done.

Thank you for seeing me, Chancellor. I teach at a village school up the valley, in a room with one window that opens. Last spring I asked the ministry for a second reader in Dravenni, and I was told the request would be considered in the next budget cycle. Children who learn their letters in a language the school does not use tend to leave early, and the ones who leave early are the ones the mines used to take.

I am not asking for the valleys to be separated from the Republic. I am asking for a governor who can speak to a mother at the school gate without an interpreter, and who will carry the valleys' complaints to the Assembly in the language the Assembly uses for its laws. I would answer to Veltria. I would also answer to the families who have never had anyone in an office who looked like them, and I think the Republic would be safer if it listened to both.

May I ask you something before you ask me anything, Chancellor? When the capital decided these valleys needed a gendarme and not a school, did anyone in Veltria ask the valleys what they wanted? When the Halden mines closed, did anyone ask the men who had dug there for three generations what they would do next? I am not asking you to answer. I am asking whether the question has ever been put in this building at all.

Would a valley govern itself with the capital at its side? Could it do so without the capital? Are those questions a threat to the Republic, or only a threat to a Republic that has never considered them? I would take them to the Assembly myself, in Dravenni if the chamber will not hear them in any other tongue. Who in Veltria is prepared to let them be asked out loud?

Three people and one province, and a border that has stayed quiet only because nobody has leaned on it. Ostrava would keep the lid on and call the silence peace. Marr would build a bridge the capital has never walked across. Vashko would hand the valleys a question the capital may not survive answering. Each of them is describing the same ground, and none of them is describing a valley the capital has tried to govern with the people in it rather than over them.

monologue: Three people, and each is right about the valleys they know. Ostrava's roads are safe and his permits are orderly, and the quiet they buy is real. Whoever you appoint will be read as Halvek's method by the Halvekist press, and it will be the first test of whether the capital means what it says about the north.

choices.text: "Keep Ostrava. The valleys stay under the permit system until I decide otherwise, and I will be reading the patrol reports myself."

reactions.text: Ostrava will take the decision as a commission to keep doing what he has always done. The valleys will take it as the capital choosing the lid again. Both readings will be accurate, and only one of them will be written down.
Marr closes the notebook on her knee. She does not argue. She looks at the map for a long moment, at the red roads and the small crosses, before she says anything at all.

choices.text: "Ilse Marr. Start with the schoolhouses and make the readers bilingual. I will defend the appointment in the Assembly as the Republic's answer to the valleys."

reactions.text: Marr lets out a breath she seems to have held since the stairs. She says she will need the schoolhouses first and the roads after, and she thanks you without ceremony, as if the decision were already a piece of work.
The Republic has an answer for the valleys that the valleys can read, and that is new. The cost is that Ostrava's men will not forgive the decision, and they will remember which office signed it.

choices.text: "Teren Vashko. The valleys deserve to be asked what they want, and I want to hear the answer from someone who will say it plainly in front of the Assembly."

reactions.text: Vashko inclines his head. He asks, quite gently, whether the Chancellor is prepared to hear what the valleys say once they are no longer being asked to be quiet. He does not wait for an answer, and he does not look triumphant.

Vyktor does not write anything down. He says the appointment is the right question to have asked and the hardest answer to hold. The valleys will remember that the capital asked. The capital will need to decide now what it does if the answer is no.
